text: A Hattar I attended a meeting with Shanghai Metals Market New Energy Department last week focused on Nickel, Copper and Lithium. They pointed out that Indonesia may reduce the nickel ore production quota, known as RKAB, for 2026 to around 250Mt to tighten supply and support nickel prices. They estimate Indonesia's nickel ore production is 265MT for 2025. That could signal a 5.6% reduction in 2026 if the quota comes to pass. Interestingly, the RKAB quota for 2025 was 326Mt, so production fell well short of the quota. Reducing the quota could be problematic for Indonesia as they bring on new nickel smelting capacity. You may already be aware that Indonesia banned raw nickel ore exports in 2020, forcing the refining and smelting of metal locally. SMM estimate that Indonesia’s nickel ore demand could reach around 280M wmt. The nut of it is that there could be reduced Indonesian ore production in 2026 but SMM remains dubious of quota reduction coming to pass. They also pointed out that mined grades of nickel ore grade declined in 2025 to an average of ~1.57% from ~1.66% in 2024 which has an impact on mining costs or profitability. The other thing I suspect will push up the cost of Indonesian produced nickel is the increasing cost of sulphuric acid which is heavily used in the processing of nickel from laterites. Sulphuric acid demand from Indonesian HPAL projects is estimated at 7.12Mt in 2025. Indonesia imports most of its sulphuric acid (or sulphur) from China and Korea. The cost of sulphuric acid from North Asia is surging, up 26.47% in November and 145.26% year-over-year. Some of the Indonesian smelters are producing acid from sulphur which has also jumped in price by 114% YoY. It was expected that The startup of Freeport McMoran's Manyar smelter in Java and AMNT's Copper Smelter  in the Nusa Tenggara province would produce at least 3Mt/yr of acid by the end of 2025 but I think that was hampered as a result of copper shortages for the smelters, partially as a result of the block cave incident at PT Freeport's Grasberg Mine. In any case, any of these things may support the price of Nickel. Nickel Futures jumped 12.25% in December.

text:
Hey guys,
Keen to hear views on tungsten from the group — a commodity that’s relatively new to me. Up until now I’ve mostly focused on copper, gold, uranium and oil & gas.
I’ve been digging into tungsten recently and wanted to sense-check my thinking with those here who know the space better.
From what I can see, tungsten is a critical defence and industrial metal (munitions, aerospace, tooling, semiconductors). The US currently has zero domestic production and is fully import-reliant, while China controls ~80–85% of global supply. Prices have recently hit record highs amid export controls, supply tightness and rising defence demand, alongside increasing discussion around strategic stockpiling and reshoring in the US and Europe. Unlike many battery metals, tungsten also appears structurally undersupplied, with limited new projects coming online.
Would really appreciate any insights, counterpoints, or resources worth reading.
Thank you in advance !

text:
Hey Team,
RE: Hot Chili Copper (ASX: HCH)
I bought HCH around $0.47 in April 2025, and at ~$1.44 it’s already up ~200%. That said, I’m really viewing this as a 2026+ story, not a short-term trade.
What’s kept me interested is the combination of a large, growing copper-gold resource in Chile, strong leverage to higher copper prices and a steady pipeline of catalysts (drilling, resource growth, studies)
When you overlay that with the amount of copper M&A we saw in 2025 (New World Resources, Xanadu, SolGold, etc.), it also feels like the sort of asset that could eventually land on a major’s radar if copper stays tight.
In terms of Valuation, I’m simply working off what the company has already outlined:
At $5/lb copper, management has spoken about an after-tax NPV of ~US$2.5B (~A$3.7B). Even applying a fairly conservative 0.3× NPV, that implies roughly $6.30/share, or about a 337% uplift from ~$1.44.
At $6/lb copper, management has indicated that every +10c adds ~US$170M in NPV, pushing total NPV closer to US$4.2B (~A$6.3B). On the same multiple, that points to $10+ per share, or roughly a 640% upside from here.
One thing I’m watching closely is Le Verde. If drilling continues to prove up higher-grade, near-surface material, it could materially improve the front end of the project — stronger early cash flow, shorter payback, and lower overall risk. Those factors tend to matter a lot to majors when assessing development or M&A potential.
Less obvious advantages
1. I also think HCH has some under-appreciated strengths that don’t always show up in headline numbers:
2. Water rights & infrastructure in an arid region — a major de-risking factor in Chile, with potential standalone optionality.
3. Coastal, low-altitude location, avoiding many of the cost, logistics and workforce challenges seen in high-Andean copper projects.
4. Good access to ports, power and roads, which should help on both capex and opex.
5. Leadership: a technically strong team with a clear development pathway and credibility in the copper space, which matters when dealing with majors, financiers and regulators.
None of this includes upside from additional discoveries, and there’s still plenty of drilling ahead.
There are obviously real risks. A global slowdown or recession would pressure copper and copper equities across the board. That said, given the scale of the resource, gold credits, water position, and what looks like a structurally tightening copper market, HCH feels well positioned if the macro holds together.
Lastly, I know Rick Rule is a shareholder and has previously commented that the project needs a high-grade starter pit— which Le Verde increasingly looks like it could be — and has also described the asset as gigantic and well located.
Keen to hear others’ views — especially anything I might be missing.
(Not financial advice. Do your own research. Just my personal opinion) 
Thank you in advance !

text:
I am so surprised nobody mentions and emphasizes that Nations Royalty holds mineral tax right royalties and not NSRs.

This is super important.

What they have is a royalty on taxes coming from the mine profits and not the revenue. Which means - no profit no royalty collected.

NSRs are so great because you don’t care if the mine is profitable or not, you collect the money anyways. This is true optionality, what Nations Royalty has - is not.

This is especially important for the KSM project that is super capex heavy. God knows when this project will register taxable profits after capex write offs, even if it is built.

 Also at 170 million market cap, Nations Royalty is not an option play on KSM. You need to bake KSM happy path into certainty to justify this valuations. That is not how optionality works.

After this many years of Rick’s education, guys, we should be able to see these red flags from miles away.

space.description:
THE GOLDEN TRIANGLE

Since Alexander Choquette first discovered gold at the confluence of the Stikine and Anuk Rivers in 1861, the region in Northwest British Columbia known as the Golden Triangle has blossomed into a transformative mining mega-district.  

Early discoveries were impressive. The Premier Gold Mine, which launched operations in 1918, produced 2 million ounces of gold and 45 million ounces of silver before closing in 1952.  

More recently, Eskay (1994-) became Canada’s highest-grade gold mine with over 3 million ounces of gold, and the world’s fifth largest silver producer with over 160 million ounces of silver. The Brucejack deposit began operations in 2017 and has produced over 1 million ounces of gold to date.  

Today, the KSM Project represents one of the largest undeveloped gold projects in the world — one study estimates the proven and probable reserves at 38.8 million ounces of gold and 10.2 billion pounds of copper.3

Augmenting this world-class geology is an impressive package of infrastructure upgrades which includes the 287 kV, 344 km Northwest Transmission Line, a major north-south artery (Highway 37), and an ice-free deep-water port in the town of Stewart.  

These factors coupled with a friendly political setting and surging commodity prices make the Golden Triangle a rare opportunity. 


Among the topics we will discuss are:

  • The rich history of the Golden Triangle region 

  • Geological factors that make this a world-class region 

  • Infrastructure considerations that can make or break a project 

  • Political environment and First Nations collaboration 

  • Economic conditions and project viability 

  • Things that could go wrong — factors to consider before investing

text:
Aya Gold & Silver Announces Record Q4 and Full Year 2025 Silver Production


Production of 5 million silver equivalent ounces for the year, including the Boumadine tailings operation
Record production of 545,491ounces at Zgounder for the month of December
MONTREAL, Jan. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aya Gold & Silver Inc. (TSX: AYA; OTCQX: AYASF) (“Aya” or the “Corporation”) is pleased to announce record quarterly production, recoveries, and throughput at its Zgounder Silver Mine in the Kingdom of Morocco for the three-month period ended December 31st, 2025.
Q4-2025 Operational Summary
Record silver production of 1.37 million (“M”) ounces (“oz”) up 2% from Q3-2025.
December 2025 record silver production at Zgounder of 545,491 oz with mill feed grade of 147g/t grams per tonne (“g/t”) silver (“Ag”).
Ore processed averaged 3,796 tonnes per day (“tpd”), representing an 14% improvement over Q3-2025 and running 41% above nameplate capacity. This includes a record average milling rate of 4,107 tpd milling rate in the month of December.
Average head grade processed of 134 g/t Ag for the quarter.
Sustained silver recovery averaged 91.2%.
Sustained high mill availability at 99.0%, underscoring consistent operational discipline and reliability.
Record underground mining rate of 1,387 tpd at 161g/t, and 2,800 tpd of ore from the open pit at 115 g/t, for a total mining rate of 4,187 tpd at 130 g/t, increasing stockpiled ore quarter-on-quarter.

“Zgounder delivered another strong quarter, with solid Q4 production, recoveries, mining rate and throughput” said Benoit La Salle, President & CEO. “The team’s efforts throughout 2025 culminated in a record December, with a milling and mining rate of 4,107 tpd and 4,652 tpd, respectively, and an all-time high silver production of 545,491oz. We also published a new mine plan aligned with the current silver price environment, positioning Zgounder to maximize cash flow. With the 2025 ramp-up complete, our focus now shifts to disciplined execution, continuous optimization, and consistent delivery into 2026 and beyond.”
Q4-2025 and 2025 Summary Production Results

Q4-2025 Operational Update 
Underground development and stope sequencing advanced during the quarter, supporting an average mining rate of 1,387 tpd at 161 g/t Ag. Underground tonnage and grade have now been on target for two consecutive quarters, positioning the mine to reach our 2026 objectives.
Open-pit operations during the quarter focused on finalising the ramp-up and reached 2,800 tpd of ore at a strip ratio of 13, for a total material movement rate of 38,814 tpd, near our long-term target of 45,000 tpd. With both mine ramp-ups completed, over 194,000 tonnes of stockpiled ore available, and record mill throughput, Zgounder is well positioned for 2026. Blast-movement control and bench-by-bench modeling were implemented in H2-2025 to maximise ore recovery and minimise external dilution. These aspects will continue to be the operational focus in 2026.
The mill processed an average of 3,796 tpd for the quarter and 3,229 tpd for the year, highlighting debottlenecking efforts at the Zgounder plant through the year. Recovery was sustained above 91% for H2-2025. Record throughput and recovery were achieved at the processing plant through improved blending, circuit optimization, and increased tailings-pumping capacity, allowing for steadier, higher-rate milling.
Finally, the Zgounder team efforts through 2025 culminated into a record month of December where the milling rate reached 4,107 tpd and the mining rate reached 4,652 tpd of ore, for an all-time high 545,491 oz of silver recovered at the plant in a single month.
Boumadine historical pyrite stockpile commercialization
In 2025, Aya started the reclaiming and sale of its historical pyrite stockpile at Boumadine. Operations started in Q4-2025 and 13,498 tonnes were reclaimed and crushed, at a grade of 192g/t Ag and 2.87 g/t Au. Total production of 1,245 oz of gold and 83,480 oz of silver was achieved, for a total of 172,129 oz of silver equivalent (AgEq1) for the year 2025.
2025 Total production Zgounder and Boumadine
In 2025, the company produced 4,829,151 oz of silver at its Zgounder mine and 172,129 oz of silver equivalent at Boumadine for a total AgEq production of 5,001,280 oz for the Corporation.
Qualified Person
The technical information contained in this press release have been reviewed and approved by Raphael Beaudoin, P. Eng, Vice-President, Operations, who is a “Qualified Person” as defined under National Instrument 43-101 – Standards of Disclosure for Mineral Projects (“NI 43-101”).
About Aya Gold & Silver Inc.
Aya Gold & Silver is a Canadian precious metals mining company anchored in Morocco and active across the full mining value chain. The Corporation has established exploration leadership through a systematic, technology-led, data-driven approach and is focused on expanding its resource base and land package along the Anti-Atlas Fault — one of Africa’s most geologically rich, underexplored and mining-friendly regions.
Aya operates Zgounder, a rare primary silver mine, and produces silver doré from its newly expanded processing facility. Aya’s growth pipeline includes the Boumadine polymetallic project, where feasibility study work is underway. The project hosts a substantial mineral resource, a large mineralized footprint and significant exploration potential.
Led by a proven team of mining professionals, Aya is guided by a vision of responsible mining and is committed to delivering sustainable value for shareholders, employees and host communities.
For additional information, please visit Aya’s website at www.ayagoldsilver.com.

text:
Have you all heard about the Donut Solid State battery? The claim is its cheaper, more durable (100,000 charge cycles), charges quicker, and has a wider thermal tolerance -3C to 100C. Essentially a revolutionary technology. Using Rick Rule's unanswered questions they only have 2 left. Do third parties validate their claims about its capabilities? (they've already sent samples out for validation) and 2. How long till they are commercially available at scale?

Now their chemistry is proprietary but we will find out what materials it's using soon (months). They have already stated it does not contain lithium and will be made of "readily available materials". This technology if true is going to be completely transformative.

You need to be aware of these changes in battery metals they will effect your portfolio. Samsung's solid state battery is being priced into silver as we speak. The entire sweet of next gen battery tech isn't far behind either. Sodium Manganese batteries for grid scale ect. One commodity I'm looking at is Nickel. About 15% of Nickel is used in batteries and appears to be being phased out. I'm not saying this to scare you away from nickel! Remember its supply & demand, Rick has pointed out many times the supply side dynamics on this commodity, it's just something we need to be aware of on a 2-5 year time line.

text:
VIZSLA COPPER PLANS AGGRESSIVE DRILL PROGRAM ACROSS THE THIRA ALTERATION CORRIDOR, POPLAR PROJECT
Vancouver, British Columbia, January 14, 2026 – Vizsla Copper Corp. (TSXV: VCU, OTCQB: VCUFF, FRANKFURT: 97E0) (“Vizsla Copper” or the “Company”) is pleased to report preparations are underway for an aggressive drill program at the Poplar Project (the “Poplar Project” or “Poplar”), central British Columbia. Up to 8,000 meters of drilling will focus on investigating the extent of the Thira porphyry copper-molybdenum discovery as well as evaluating new targets across the extensive +8 kilometer long, Thira alteration corridor.
HIGHLIGHTS
·      Significant follow-up drill program: Up to 8,000 meters of drilling across ~16 drill holes designed to build on significant results from 2025, including the discovery of the Thira porphyry copper-molybdenum zone (237.3 meters of 0.51% CuEq* (0.36% Cu, 0.02% Mo, 1.19 g/t Ag, and 0.06 g/t Au) from 117.7 meters downhole in TH25-145).
·      Expansion of the Thira discovery: One drill rig will investigate the extent and the structural and/or lithological controls on strong porphyry-related copper-molybdenum mineralization at the Thira discovery.
·      Explore for other porphyry systems: One drill rig will evaluate two recently defined targets along trend from the Thira discovery associated with the extensive Thira alteration corridor.
·      Program to commence: The two drill rigs are scheduled to mobilise in the coming weeks, with drilling to commence in the first week of February.
"With a strong treasury, fantastic targets, and copper hitting $6 per pound, 2026 is shaping up to be the most exciting year to date for Vizsla Copper" commented Craig Parry, Chairman and CEO. "Thira discovery expansion is up first for our year-round exploration plans for 2026. Look for constant news flow as our winter drill season in British Columbia transitions to our summer drill program at Palmer." 
“We are excited to kick off 2026 with a winter drill program at our Thira discovery” commented Steve Blower, VP, Exploration. “We have planned an aggressive two rig drill program that will extend known copper-molybdenum mineralization at the Thira discovery as well as evaluate new targets recently refined with ground geophysics and soil geochemistry.”
Drill Plans
The Phase 1, 2026 drill program at Poplar will consist of up to 8,000 meters of core drilling within the extensive Thira alteration corridor (Figure 1). Drilling is designed with two primary objectives:
1)      Investigate the lateral and vertical extent of known porphyry-related copper-molybdenum mineralization at the Thira Discovery. Results from the 2025 discovery drill program highlight a zone of near-surface, porphyry-related copper-molybdenum-silver-gold mineralization (e.g., 237.3 meters of 0.51% CuEq* (0.36% Cu, 0.02% Mo, 1.19 g/t Ag, and 0.06 g/t Au from 117.7 meters downhole in TH25-145, see October 20th, 2025 News Release) that spans at least 800 meters east-west and at least 500 meters north-south. Planned step-out holes in all directions are designed to constrain the scale of the porphyry system. Drilling will also investigate the structural and/or lithological controls on higher-grade copper mineralization (e.g., 77.0 meters of 0.55% CuEq* (0.43% Cu, 0.01% Mo, 1.48 g/t Ag, and 0.09 g/t Au) from 124.0 meters downhole in TH25-145) within the Thira porphyry system.
2)      Test for porphyry-related copper-molybdenum mineralization at two recently defined high-priority targets (Copper Pond and Camp Lake) situated along trend from the Thira discovery (Figure 2). Both target areas are highlighted by inverted chargeability and resistivity models derived from compiled 2024 and 2025 DCIP (direct current induced polarization) data (Figure 2). The targets are characterised by zones of moderate-chargeability response surrounded by zones of very high-chargeability which extend to depth in the 3D models. These patterns are similar to the Thira discovery (Figure 2) where a center of chalcopyrite-molybdenite bearing potassic alteration (moderate chargeability) is surrounded by a broad zone of highly-chargeable, pyrite-bearing phyllic alteration. These targets have yet to be systematically drill tested.
Timeline
Two drill rigs are planned to mobilise to site in the coming weeks.  Drilling is scheduled to begin in the first week of February.
*Copper  equivalent calculation (CuEq) uses metal prices of: Cu US$4.00/lb, Mo  US$20.00/lb, Au US$2,000/oz and Ag US$22/oz and conceptual recoveries of Cu:  80%, Mo: 80%, Au: 70% and Ag: 65%. Metallurgical test work has not been  performed on core from Thira, therefore it is uncertain which metals would  report to potential concentrates - recoveries are conceptual in nature. CuEq is  provided for illustrative purpose only to show the combined grades of Cu, Mo,  Au and Ag relative to copper price net of conceptual metallurgical recoveries.  CuEq% = Cu% + (Au g/t x (Au recovery / Cu recovery) x [Au price US$/oz ÷ 31] /  [Cu price US$/lb x 22.04623]) + (Ag g/t x (Ag recovery / Cu recovery) x [Ag  price US$/oz ÷ 31] / [Cu price US$/lb x 22.04623] + (Mo grade % x (Mo recovery  / Cu recovery) x [Mo price US$/lb x 2204.623] / [Cu price US$/lb x 2204.623]).  Composite intervals are calculated using length-weighted averages above the  cutoff grades noted above, with up to 10 meters of internal dilution. True  thickness of the bulk-tonnage style, stockwork-hosted mineralization is  unknown.
Figure 1. Map of the Poplar Project showing the location of the Thira target area and previously acquired MobileMT data1. The area circled around the apparent conductivity-high anomaly marks the footprint of the Thira alteration corridor which is the focus of the upcoming 8,000 meter drill program.
Figure 2. Map showing chargeability results (100 meter depth plan) from the new 3D inverted chargeability model with data compiled from 2024 (see January 15th, 2025 News Release) and 2025 (see November 25th, 2025 News Release) DCIP surveys across the Thira alteration corridor. Priority drill targets to be evaluated in the upcoming 8,000 meter drill program include Thira, Camp Lake and Copper Pond. Locations of the key target areas are shown as well as locations of historical shallow drill holes. Results from holes TH25-138 and TH25-145 were previously released (see July 22, 2025 and October 20, 2025 news releases). See references below for sources of historical data2,3.
Poplar Project
The 44,200-hectare Poplar project in central BC covers Mesozoic aged arc-related volcanic, sedimentary and intrusive rocks considered prospective for porphyry-related copper and gold mineralization. In addition to the Thira target, the project also hosts the Poplar deposit, a near-surface porphyry-related copper and gold system. The Thira target is approximately 10 km south of the Poplar deposit. Vizsla Copper has the option to earn a 100% interest in the property through a series of expenditure commitments and annual cash payments until 2027.

text:
I watched Steve Barton and Rick Rule last Q&A and someone asked about whether or not a certain multiple works for First Majestic at current silver prices.

I took it upon myself to use ChatGPT and copy every word Rick used and asked AI to break down what he was saying.

"I need you to explain this statement by Rick Rule when someone asked how should a miner like First Majestic who could produce around $1B in FCF with current silver prices, while having an EV of $10B and wondering if 10 times FCF multiple considered reasonable?

Rick states its reasonable by base street but is a stupid metric because it doesn't take in reserve life. You could have a short reserve life that's delivering a $1B a year for three years and is valued at $10B which means that you have seven years of penury after three good years. Valuation needs to be done on a NAV to EV basis. NAV is usually a NPV test but the discounted net present value test leaves off the cash flow tail. Cash produced after eight years doesn't have a NPV until you receive it in which case it has a great NPV. It also doesn't take into account reinvestment. So in addition to looking at NAV to EV, you have to look at the companies recycle ratio. Recycle being the amounts the number of units of reserve that they can add for the margin that they receive for selling one unit. As example, if First Majestic sells an ounce of silver for $50 and their cost to produce that ounce of silver is $25, their gross margin is $25. Recycle ratio would be the number of ounces that they could add to the balance sheet either through acquisition, exploration, or development on the margin from the $25 from the last ounce. Traditionally, companies whose recycle ratio is 1.25 to 1.3 are companies after G&A that described as having positive recycle ratios. In the silver business, everybody in the business with the exception of the top 5 or 6 have a negative recycle ratios. Break down what Rick is saying"
Rick is making two related points:
A simple EV/FCF multiple can be “reasonable” but still economically wrong
Saying “10× FCF” is “reasonable by Bay Street” just means it’s a common shorthand investors use.
Rick calls it “stupid” because FCF is a flow, and the multiple ignores the duration of that flow.
Miners are depleting businesses: every ounce produced reduces the remaining inventory (reserves/resources).
His reserve-life thought experiment
If a miner produces $1B of FCF for only 3 years (because reserves run out) and the company is valued at $10B EV, you’re paying for something like “10 years of $1B/yr” but only getting 3 years.
After year 3, unless they replace ounces, you get “seven years of penury”: the business shrinks hard or dies.
So the multiple can look fine in the moment (especially at peak silver prices) while the underlying asset base is melting.
What he wants you to do instead: tie value to the life of the orebody and the depletion schedule, not just the current cash flow snapshot.
NAV/EV (and how NAV is built) is closer to the right framework
Why NAV/EV
NAV is meant to represent the value of the operating assets over their life (and sometimes beyond, depending on how you model expansion/exploration).
EV is what the market is asking you to pay (equity + debt – cash).
So NAV/EV tells you whether you’re paying cheap or expensive relative to the asset value, not relative to one year of cash flow.
His critique of NPV-based NAV (“NPV test leaves off the cash-flow tail”)
Most sell-side NAVs are NPV(5%) or NPV(8%) of mine plan cash flows. Two issues Rick highlights:
A) Discounting makes long-dated cash flows look tiny
Cash earned in year 12, 15, 20 gets discounted so heavily that it contributes little to NPV today.
But if the mine actually survives and produces that cash, it ends up being very real cash later.
His phrasing is basically: “NPV says it’s worth little today, but when you actually receive it, it’s obviously valuable.”
Translation: NPV can understate long-life optionality (especially for assets that can be extended or expanded).
B) NPV often under-models reinvestment reality
Mines don’t just sit there; to keep producing they need:
exploration to convert resources to reserves,
development capex to open new zones,
acquisitions,
sustaining capital.
A static NPV of the existing mine plan can miss the fact that the company must reinvest to replace depletion, and that reinvestment might be cheap (good business) or expensive/destructive (bad business).
So he’s saying: NAV/EV is better than EV/FCF, but you still have to be careful about what NAV includes/excludes.
Recycle ratio: the missing “capital efficiency” test for reserve replacement
This is Rick’s practical way to judge whether the company can turn today’s margins into tomorrow’s reserves.
Definition (what he means)
If the company sells 1 oz for $50 and it costs $25 to produce, the gross margin is $25/oz.
The recycle question:
How many ounces of new reserve can they add using that $25 margin from the last ounce they mined?
That “reserve addition” can come from:
exploration (drilling and converting),
development (moving resources into mineable reserves),
acquisitions (buying ounces in the ground).
So recycle ratio is essentially a reserve replacement efficiency metric:
Recycle ratio > 1.0 = you can replace more than 1 oz for every 1 oz you produce (you’re growing inventory).
Recycle ratio ~ 1.0 = you can roughly replace what you mine (you sustain).
Recycle ratio < 1.0 = you can’t replace depletion (you shrink, unless you dilute shareholders or overpay for M&A).
Why he says “1.25–1.3 after G&A is positive”
He’s telling you the minimum needed for a healthy producer is not just “replace 1:1,” but replace with a buffer because:
G&A exists,
exploration is uncertain,
some reserve adds will be lower quality or higher cost,
you need growth to offset inevitable operational hiccups.
So a “good” miner converts margin into reserves at >1.25× type rates (roughly: a strong compounding machine).
Why he says most silver miners have negative recycle ratios
In silver, many companies:
operate at higher costs,
have shorter reserve lives,
struggle to find/convert ounces cheaply,
or overpay for acquisitions when prices are hot.
Result: their margin doesn’t buy enough future ounces. They may look amazing at peak prices (high FCF), but they’re not self-renewing businesses.
The integrated takeaway (what Rick wants you to stop doing and start doing)
Stop
Treating miners like steady perpetuities and valuing them on EV/FCF alone, especially at a cyclical peak.
Start
Evaluate three things together:
Asset duration:
How long do current reserves support production at planned rates?
What’s the real “runway” before depletion bites?
NAV/EV (properly understood):
Is the market price cheap/expensive versus the asset value?
Are you missing tail optionality or ignoring reinvestment needs?
Recycle ratio (reserve replacement economics):
Can the company replace depletion without shareholder dilution or value-destructive M&A?
Do they convert margins into new reserves at >1.25× type rates, or are they shrinking?
If a company has high current FCF but short reserve life and poor recycle ratio, Rick’s view is that a “reasonable” multiple can still be a trap: you’re paying for a long-lived cash machine, but you’re actually buying a short-lived liquidation with a great quarter.

text:
Food for thought: J. Rickards often argues that gold does not go up or down in value; it is an element of the periodic table with atomic number 79, and one ounce will be the same today as it will be in five thousand years. What changes over time is the dollar price of gold. We get it.
However, I would argue that the value of owning an ounce of gold (or silver) is not constant across the board. Without loss of generality, let’s examine the experience of the past four months through the lens of silver.
We all understand that paper silver does not have the same value as physical silver, so let’s move past that point and focus specifically on owning physical silver in the Americas. My thesis is that the value of owning physical silver varies materially depending on jurisdiction, storage, and other practical constraints.
Jurisdictions without a real market
Physical silver has significantly less value in countries where there is no functioning bullion market and the only buyers are pawn shops, which are often willing to pay less than 70% of spot. One could argue that the metal could be shipped abroad, but in practice this is extremely difficult. Securing DHL, FedEx, or any premium parcel service—with full insurance—for shipments exceeding USD 10,000 is nearly impossible unless one is a commercial entity.
Export controls
No further comment is needed on holding physical metal in countries with export restrictions or "shady" governments.
Vaulted physical silver
Let’s now consider silver stored in professional vaults.
Large countries without a strong reputation for respecting private property rights—while admittedly a harder distinction to make nowadays—are, in my view, a no-go zone.
United States. With silver being upgraded to a critical mineral of national security importance, it is reasonable to question whether the government will permanently keep its hands off privately vaulted metal if the race with China (and Mexico as the largest producer of silver) goes from sour to bitter.
Canada. In my view, this is the best option. Holding silver through private vaults or through PHYS—stored at the Royal Canadian Mint—makes sense. It is arguably less likely that Canada would take actions that could severely damage its international reputation. Yes, Canada has taken questionable actions in the recent past, but I am inclined to give the country the benefit of the doubt and interpret those actions as being more related to conforming to the behavior of a distorted peer group such as the G7.
While I am not a political analyst (I am not Canadian either), Prime Minister Carney has stated that “this is a dislocation, not a transition,” referring to Canada’s relationship with the United States—and, by extension, the G7. My interpretation is that countries are increasingly likely to act independently, prioritizing their own interests rather than mirroring their neighbors’ policies.
Canada is extremely resource-rich, and it is far easier to raise the standard of living for approximately 40 million people than for approximately 400 million in the United States or 130 million in Mexico.
Europe, by contrast, is a no-go zone. It is lost. Asia is simply too far away. Switzerland could work, but it feels like an island surrounded by hungry sharks.
On that basis, I am betting on owning physical silver stored in Canadian vaults.
Any other classmates care to jump into this discussion?

text:
On Sunday I posted three charts that signaled to me oil and oil equities are breaking out into at least a short term uptrend. Today I’m going to tell you how I’m deploying capital to this space. But first, I don’t see anything in the charts that suggest natural gas stocks are poised for gains, that could change.

As I’ve reported my PM stocks are above my max weighting so that’s where most of the capital is coming from. I definitely don’t want to sell stocks (or ETF’s) that are “working” and put the capital in stocks that aren’t working. So I’m looking for oil stocks that are breaking out of solid bases to new highs or are already in solid uptrends. I’m not looking for deep value plays, P/NAV = 0.1, that aren’t working now. I want an RSI about 0.55-0.70, mildly over bought. I’m not putting money into stocks that are overbought (RSI>0.75) and due for a pullback.

I have my watch list of 20-30 companies I like and I’m going to be scanning them daily for good entry prices (a pullback to a trend line or 20SMA) or a break from consolidation to a new high.

To the extent the short term trend keeps going, I may buy some deeper value plays where I think the market hasn’t recognized the value the company offers. But I definitely don’t want a lot of capital waiting for Godot to show up.

Stocks that fit the bill, many US and Canadian majors and the bigger oil service stocks.

I’ll be keeping an eye on the gas plays but for now, they’re most “a pair of twos” and I’m not betting on them.

text:
I hope everyone here understands the incredible opportunity this commodity bull market is giving us and to not waste it (Please God, give me one more bull market, I promise not to waste it this time).

I was fortunate early in my investing career to double my assets between Dec97 and Dec99. Fortunate because a) I piled into tech stocks early and b) I TOOK PROFITS so I didn’t give them all back. I had little idea what I was doing but I had stocks that went up 4x-5x in weeks and instinctively I sold. And I used the cash to accelerate my mortgage payments and to start my PM stack (non-correlated assets, vida infra). When your gains seem too good to be true, they probably are. That early double on my assets set me up for a lifetime of wealth building.

2025 was a great year for my portfolio, the third best in my 35 years investing. We’re only three weeks into 2026 and I’ve already achieved 47% of the gains I made in all of 2025. 4.5x of what my wife makes in a year, I made in three weeks. And I’m selling into this freaking amazing bull and putting some into oil stocks, some into bonds and some to charity.

Not me, not Rick Rule, not Lobo Tigre, not Adrian Day, not anybody can tell you how far this bull market will go. But I can tell you take they agree that you must some profits along the way and put them into non-correlated assets. Taking profits from gold miner A and putting them into gold miner B isn’t taking profits.

Pasting here what I posted in my Substack chat a few days ago on Hochshild Mining:
“Hi – Looking back at Hochschild Mining‘s (silver and gold producer) production results and guidance unveiled yesterday… This is a stock we own. Vs our expectations into the event, production figures were mildly weaker though the Mara Rosa mine which had been the key reason for guidance cuts last year was in line which is reassuring. Costs however, were higher across the board – but on a gold equivalent basis, all-in sustaining costs remain less than half the current spot price.
At say $60/oz silver and $4200 gold, the stock is on c10% equity free cashflow (EqFCF) yield and presents 30% upside (1x NAV 9% WACC). Instead, at spot prices ($4800/oz gold, $93/oz silver), the stock is on 17% EqFCF yield and would indicate a double in value in from here.
While silver stocks are getting less cheap, select silver equities offer better risk reward than the metal.”
Looking indeed at doubles from here on some of the (larger) silver stocks without the need for higher metals p… seems consistent with Rick’s view on risk/reward for the equities here.

text:
Hey guys, serious question looking at the next 5–10 years: If you’re actually going to put money into Argentina right now, what do you pick — real estate, productive farmland, or oil & gas assets (Vaca Muerta related)?
Real estate has a very obvious tailwind around Vaca Muerta: massive housing shortage for workers, Añelo and surrounding areas are screaming for thousands more beds/units, forecasts say the deficit could hit 30,000+ homes by 2030. Classic supply-demand imbalance while the shale boom keeps running.
Oil & gas / Vaca Muerta stakes feel more like a dividend & export story: production is smashing records, energy trade surplus exploding, many expect US$25–37 bn in annual exports by 2030 — potentially overtaking agriculture as the main FX earner. But very cyclical (oil price), huge capex needed for pipelines/LNG, and politically sensitive.
Farmland is the old-school “hard asset” Argentina bet: incredible soil, water access, established know-how — and Milei already cut export taxes and removed most foreign ownership restrictions on rural land. Steady cash flow from soy, corn, wheat etc., but exposed to weather, global commodity prices and — down the road — maybe disruptive tech.
Big caveat for all three: once you’re in, you’re basically locked in — very illiquid, exiting cleanly is tough and often painful. Future wildcards (AI/robotics in ag, Bill Gates-style vertical farming factories, synthetic food etc.) can only be treated as a big unknown risk factor right now.
What would you prioritize and why?

text:
GSilver (GSVF) thesis (Q3’25) — the upside is metals… the risk is execution + debt + dilution
Let me be clear: this stock is torque. If silver and gold stay high, the upside can be nasty in a good way. But this isn’t a “clean” miner. It’s a company with real leverage to precious metals and real problems that can ruin the upside if they don’t execute.
What the report actually shows
Q3 wasn’t weak because metals were low. Metals were already strong.
·         They realized about $39.03/oz silver and $3,441.75/oz gold in Q3.
·         They sold 280,511 oz silver, 2,263 oz gold, plus lead and zinc from Topia.
So why was the quarter ugly?
Because production dropped:
·         They had a 41% decrease in tonnes milled and 41% reduction in AgEq ounces produced.
And when tonnage drops, unit costs go crazy:
·         Q3 cash cost was $32.10/AgEq oz and AISC was $40.64/AgEq oz.
That’s the whole story: execution and throughput.
The upside case (why I’m even looking at this)
Now fast forward to today’s metals market.
Silver and gold have moved into a different regime. If they can sell the same ounces they sold in Q3, but at today’s pricing environment, the revenue doesn’t go up 10%… it can go up 2×+. That’s what operating leverage is.
And here’s what’s important:
Costs don’t rise dollar-for-dollar with metal prices.
So the incremental price mostly drops to cash flow — assuming the mines are running.
That’s the upside: same ounces, higher price, big margin expansion.
The part people ignore (why it’s a double-edged sword)
Their debt is tied to gold.
·         The Ocean Partners facility is repayable in fixed gold ounces (or USD equivalent), using LBMA pricing mechanics.
·         That obligation has an embedded derivative marked to fair value.
So when gold rises:
·         yes, revenue potential improves,
·         but the value of what they owe also rises, and you can get quarters where metals are up and the income statement still looks messy.
So you don’t get the full gold upside cleanly. It’s still upside — just not smooth.
Pros (what I actually like from the report)
·         Realized prices were already strong in Q3, so the business has real leverage when it runs.
·         They sell four metals (Ag, Au, Pb, Zn). That helps stability.
·         They acknowledge the bottlenecks and say they’re taking steps, including acquiring additional equipment in Q4 2025.
·         Bolanitos can be a real catalyst if it adds stable tonnage/margins: up to $50M, with $30M cash + $10M shares upfront.
Cons (what can absolutely wreck shareholders)
·         Production volatility is the #1 risk. Q3 proved it.
·         AISC is high, and AISC includes corporate drag + sustaining capex + other all-in items.
·         Gold-linked debt/derivatives can “tax” the upside.
·         Operational/legal friction: they had bank accounts frozen in Mexico and $2.403M restricted cash, still frozen after quarter end.
·         Dilution is part of the deal: bought deal 87M units at CAD$0.50 with half-warrants at CAD$0.65. Plus Bolanitos includes shares in the purchase price.
My conclusion (straight)
GSilver is a high-beta precious metals play. If silver and gold stay elevated and they stabilize throughput, the upside can be big because the leverage is real.
But I’m not pretending this is low risk:
·         If they keep missing tonnage, costs stay high and the leverage disappears.
·         If dilution keeps stacking, shareholders don’t get paid even if the company “grows.”
·         And gold-linked debt means the gold upside isn’t fully yours.
So the thesis is simple:
This is not a “quality” miner. This is a torque play.
The upside is there because metals are in a different market now — but they have to execute, and the capital structure matters.
